title: Using Fuels Safely
description: Lord Cinder preys on careless fuel use. Learn to handle fuels safely to earn the final ember before the showdown.

content.value: Fuels store a lot of energy, which makes them useful but also potentially dangerous. Handling them safely prevents fires, burns and poisoning. A few simple rules keep everyone safe.

FUEL SAFETY RULES
🪟  keep cooking areas well ventilated (fresh air)
🚫  never leave a flame or stove unattended
👃  if you smell gas: turn off the supply, open windows, no flames/switches
🧯  keep a fire extinguisher or sand nearby
👨‍👩‍👧  children should use fuels only with an adult

If a fuel burns with too LITTLE oxygen, it burns incompletely and produces CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) — a poisonous gas that has no smell and can be deadly. This is why we must never burn coal or run a generator in a closed room. Good ventilation is essential.

Burning any fuel uses up oxygen and can release harmful gases. Keeping the space well-ventilated ensures enough oxygen for complete burning and lets dangerous gases escape. This single habit prevents many accidents.
Carbon monoxide (CO) is called a 'silent killer' because it has no colour or smell. Always burn fuels in a well-ventilated space, and never in a closed room while sleeping.

Key Takeaway: Fuels must be handled safely — with good ventilation, never left unattended, and away from careless flames. Incomplete burning produces poisonous carbon monoxide, so fresh air is essential.

quiz.question: Burning a fuel with too little oxygen produces the poisonous gas…
quiz.explain: Incomplete burning (too little oxygen) produces poisonous carbon monoxide.

quiz.question: Why is good ventilation important when burning fuels?
options: It supplies oxygen for complete burning and lets harmful gases escape
quiz.explain: Ventilation provides enough oxygen for complete combustion and removes dangerous gases.

quiz.question: Carbon monoxide is especially dangerous because it…
options: has no colour or smell (a 'silent killer')
quiz.explain: CO is colourless and odourless, so you can't detect it — hence 'silent killer'.
